title: Things That Help: Five Tips for Better PD This (Crazy) School Year
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing to both PD organizers and PD attendees during the disorienting first pandemic-era school year, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that most professional development advice misses the real problem: a self-reinforcing whirlpool of rising workload and rising pressure that leaves teachers too reactive to absorb new ideas. He urges PD leaders to name that dynamic honestly, to offer optional sessions on workload management and boundaries, and to feature short videos from modestly successful (not superstar) teachers describing what is actually working for them, since ordinary practitioners are more relatable and more replicable than burnout-prone overachievers. He also recommends blending asynchronous pre-work with synchronous sessions so teachers retain some autonomy over their time. For teachers on the receiving end of imperfect PD, he counsels extending grace to overwhelmed organizers and refocusing attention on one's own core purpose for the year. The piece closes with a reminder that even amid chaos, teachers control more than it feels like they do.
points: Context should drive PD design this year: the real barrier isn't format (in-person vs. remote) but the internal workload-pressure whirlpool that leaves teachers too reactive to learn.

PD organizers get more traction from short videos by modestly successful (not superstar) teachers sharing 2-3 concrete things that are helping, since over-polished exemplars don't relate to struggling peers and can normalize unsustainable overwork.
Blending asynchronous prework with synchronous sessions restores a measure of autonomy to teachers during a year when so much feels dictated by circumstance.
For PD recipients, extending grace to imperfect organizers frees up attention to refocus on the single clearest statement of what matters most in one's own practice.
quotes: Instead, think deeply on the inner landscape of your teachers. Not just that they are struggling, but why they are struggling — what the inner dynamic is like. You know as well as I do that your teachers don't want another person telling them that it's hard; what they want is help!

Left to itself, this double whammy acts recursively, reinforcing itself in the worst way. The pressure leads to poorer thinking — performance always declines amidst too much pressure — and poorer thinking makes us prone to living in a suboptimal reactive mode.

Find the handful of teachers who are not miserable right now and are working sustainably and aren't mailing it in, and ask them to screencast themselves talking through 2-3 things that are helping them right now.

Now notice: I said "modestly successful" teachers because you don't want to always have videos from the people known as "the best," and you especially don't want videos from people who are working 90+ hours per week to produce their success.
The better you can do at getting people who are in it in front of your teachers, the better the PD is likely to be received. This is always true, but especially so in times of stress.
Keep in mind that the people in charge of PD in your school system are having a hard time right now, too. Workload and pressure? We don't have a monopoly on that.
We only control what we can control — but gosh, what we do control is a lot.
